action_criteria.rationale: Contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion and FLAIR is the standard imaging for a suspected diffuse glioma: it defines the enhancing target, the oedema and the mass effect, and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the left temporal mass causes midline shift and ambient cistern compression, and the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
Do not start radiotherapy, temozolomide or other tumour-directed therapy before the integrated tissue diagnosis is established.
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given the planned neurosurgery and bleeding risk.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left temporal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping, with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Before gadolinium MRI and contrast CT, review the prior contrast reaction: a prior reaction to iodinated contrast is not a contraindication to gadolinium; for contrast CT give corticosteroid and antihistamine premedication or use an alternative study [ACR_contrast].

Investigate the sodium of 129 mmol/L before dexamethasone and surgery: assess volume status, serum and urine osmolality and urine sodium, restrict fluid if the picture is SIADH, and correct by no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.
Stop as-needed ibuprofen before neurosurgery and while on dexamethasone (platelet inhibition and gastrointestinal bleeding risk); use paracetamol for headache.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 54 with KPS 80, the standard is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021); with an unmethylated MGMT promoter the benefit of temozolomide is smaller, so clinical trial options should also be discussed.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Carmen Herrera is a 54-year-old right-handed woman and IT project manager who presents with a two-month history of progressive difficulty finding words during work meetings, accompanied by subtle personality changes noticed primarily by her husband. Her husband reports that approximately two months ago, she began pausing more frequently during dinner conversations, searching for words that would normally come easily to her. As a project manager who regularly presented to clients, she had always been articulate, and these pauses were immediately noticeable to her family and eventually to her colleagues. Over the past month, the word-finding difficulty has worsened, and she has started using circumlocutions — describing objects rather than naming them. Her husband also reports that she has become unusually irritable and short-tempered over the past six weeks, which is quite unlike her typically patient demeanor. She has had two episodes of unprovoked crying at work, leading to embarrassment and contributing to her decision to take medical leave one week ago. She describes a dull, persistent left-sided headache that developed approximately three weeks ago, which she initially attributed to stress and treated with ibuprofen. Unlike her typical migraines, this headache is constant rather than episodic, is not associated with photophobia or phonophobia, and only partially responds to her usual analgesics. She denies any nausea or vomiting. She has also noticed increasing fatigue and difficulty concentrating while reviewing project documents, tasks she previously managed with ease. There has been no witnessed seizure activity, no episodes of loss of consciousness, and no visual disturbances that she has recognized, although her husband noted she has been bumping into doorframes on her right side more frequently over the past two weeks. She denies any fevers, weight loss, night sweats, or new skin lesions. She has no history of cancer and no known exposures to carcinogens. Her primary care physician initially attributed her symptoms to depression and work-related burnout, but after failing to improve on a short trial of sertraline and given the progressive nature of her symptoms, he obtained a non-contrast CT of the head, which showed a left temporal hypodensity with surrounding oedema and slight midline shift, prompting urgent referral and admission.

neurological_exam.additional: No papilledema on fundoscopic examination. No meningismus. Mild difficulty with phonemic fluency (generates 8 words starting with 'F' in 60 seconds, below expected for education level). Semantic fluency relatively preserved (14 animals in 60 seconds).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements mildly slowed on the right compared to the left but no frank dysdiadochokinesia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive. Visual fields: subtle right upper quadrantanopia on confrontation testing, confirmed with finger counting in the right upper field — patient consistently misses 2 of 5 stimuli. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. No ptosis. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Mild right lower facial weakness noted on emotional expression but symmetric on volitional smile. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength full.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady, normal base. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Appears mildly anxious but cooperative. Attention grossly intact — performs serial sevens accurately (5 of 5). Language is fluent but notable for occasional word-finding pauses, particularly for low-frequency words. She circumlocutes when unable to retrieve the target word (e.g., says 'the thing you write with' instead of 'pen'). Repetition intact. Follows complex three-step commands. Reading and writing intact. MMSE 27/30 — loses 2 points on delayed recall (recalls 1 of 3 objects spontaneously, 1 with category cue, fails 1) and 1 point on naming (correctly names watch but calls stethoscope 'the doctor's listening thing').
neurological_exam.motor: Right upper extremity: 5-/5 grip strength, 4+/5 finger abduction, 5/5 deltoid, biceps, and triceps. Right lower extremity: 5/5 throughout. Left upper and lower extremities: 5/5 throughout. No pronator drift. No fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Right biceps 2+, triceps 2+, brachioradialis 2+, patellar 2+, Achilles 2+. Left biceps 2+, triceps 2+, brachioradialis 2+, patellar 2+, Achilles 2+. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact bilaterally. Pinprick intact. Proprioception intact at fingers and toes. No sensory extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
